item.text:
{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","answer":"NAD(P) binding is a biochemical capability that evolved in multiple structural contexts, not a marker of one universal homologous lineage. In SCOPe 2.08, the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold superfamily c.2.1 (SUNID 51735) belongs to fold c.2, whereas the NAD(P)-linked oxidoreductase superfamily c.1.7 (SUNID 51430) belongs to the TIM beta/alpha-barrel fold c.1. Both fall within the alpha/beta class c; that broad architectural similarity does not establish common ancestry.

This distribution supports independent recruitment or convergent evolution of cofactor binding across distinct lineages, alongside divergent evolution within homologous families and superfamilies. Different classifications alone do not prove independent origins or exclude extremely ancient homology. SCOPe families group clearly related proteins; superfamilies express probable common ancestry even when sequence similarity is weak. A shared fold describes structural topology without necessarily implying homology, and class describes still broader secondary-structure organization.

Cofactor chemistry constrains binding sites: unrelated proteins can independently develop similar phosphate-binding loops, hydrogen bonds, charged residues, and nicotinamide positioning. Short motifs or locally similar catalytic geometries can therefore reflect chemical necessity rather than inheritance. Establishing homology requires broader evidence, such as statistically significant sequence/profile similarity spanning the domain, conserved topology and detailed structural correspondence beyond the active site, and consistent evolutionary relationships.

Neither NAD(P) binding nor a similar active site alone justifies transferring substrate specificity, reaction mechanism, NAD-versus-NADP preference, or a homology-modeling template. Such transfers require appropriate domain-wide relationships and, for precise functional claims, biochemical or ligand-bound structural evidence. One NAD(P)-binding representative cannot stand for all of these folds or superfamilies.","evidence_used":["Pretrained knowledge of protein evolution and SCOPe hierarchy","mcp__scope__get_scop_node","/api/v1/releases/current","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.2","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.2.1","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.1.7","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.1.7/parents"]}]}
